title: Lean Community Backs AI-Assisted Riemann Hypothesis Proof
excerpt: Levent Alpöge’s work with Claude has passed substantial independent checks. The challenge now is to turn a verified result into mathematical understanding.
imageAlt: Historical portrait of Bernhard Riemann wearing spectacles and a dark suit, with his signature and the date 1863 below
imageCaption: Bernhard Riemann, 1863. Unidentified photographer; Smithsonian Institution Libraries, Dibner Library’s Scientific Identity collection (SIL14-R003-02). Original collection record · Image and reuse record: no known copyright restrictions. Wikimedia’s resized scan; no AI-generated imagery.
content:
On November 20, 2026, mathematician Levent Alpöge announced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis developed with Claude, releasing the argument in Lean, a formal proof assistant. One day later, the Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative publicly endorsed its correctness. For a problem that has shaped mathematics since 1859, that combination of discovery and independent verification deserves serious attention. Alpöge’s announcement · Community verification statement

Why this is such a big deal

The Riemann Hypothesis concerns the zeros of the Riemann zeta function: its nontrivial zeros should all have real part one-half. Behind that compact statement lies a profound question about prime numbers. The prime number theorem describes their average distribution; the hypothesis controls how far their actual distribution can stray from that average. Resolving it would settle a central question about the structure of the integers, 167 years after Riemann posed it. Clay Mathematics Institute’s explanation

The verified scope also includes the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions. That is a substantial extension, but it should be described precisely: the published verification does not cover every broader conjecture that goes under the GRH label, including general automorphic L-functions. Scope of the checked theorems

What the Lean community actually checked

The community’s endorsement goes well beyond observing that some code runs. Its November 21 statement says, “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.” Reviewers checked the established Mathlib formulation, reproduced compilation, compared the submitted theorem against that formulation, and checked the exported proof with multiple proof checkers. These address the obvious concerns: proving a different statement, introducing hidden assumptions, or exploiting a particular checker. The four verification criteria

Andrew Sutherland’s MIT verification record, last updated November 24 at 05:25 UTC when consulted for this article, reports successful checks by Lean’s own kernels and independent implementations, along with a separate sandboxed rebuild reproducing the proof export byte for byte. The headline theorems use only Lean’s three standard axioms. One additional end-to-end verification run remained listed as running; several other checks had already passed. These are reported verification results, not computations independently rerun by OpenScientific. MIT verification files and logs

The jokes need context

Alpöge’s online presentation has made an already unusual announcement harder to interpret. In his November 23 X post, he wrote: “250,000+ pages was a joke guys!” He apologized for the confusion and acknowledged that the Lean submission needed cleanup. That clarification concerns the page-count spectacle and the quality of the presentation; it does not retract the mathematical result. The approximately 17 million lines reported by the Lean community are a separate measure of the released formal library. Alpöge’s clarification · The community’s codebase description

In a follow-up, he pushed back against readers treating his comments as an admission of a faulty proof: “No? It literally checked out days ago?” His tone is informal, but the underlying distinction is sound. An awkward announcement and a cumbersome argument can deserve criticism while the evidence for correctness remains strong.

Where skepticism still belongs

Formal verification establishes deductions from specified definitions and axioms. It does not automatically tell mathematicians which ideas are essential, which steps can be removed, or why the argument works at a conceptual level. In his announcement, Alpöge acknowledges that he has not mastered all the surrounding mathematics and commits to understanding, explaining and simplifying the work. Those are substantial responsibilities. They are also different from the claim that a lengthy or unattractive proof must be false. Alpöge on explanation and simplification

The credit should be shared accurately, too. Alpöge describes guiding the investigation and Claude making striking advances near the end. His account supports calling this a human–AI collaboration; it does not establish that an unattended chatbot independently solved the problem. The author’s account of the collaboration

Formal endorsement also should not be confused with a Millennium Prize award. Clay’s rules require publication in a qualifying outlet, at least two years after publication, and general acceptance in the mathematics community before consideration. That process has its own standards and timeline. Clay’s prize rules

A reason for measured optimism

Our view is that Alpöge and the Lean community have earned a presumption of serious engagement. The constructive response is to examine the public evidence, reproduce it where possible, and extract an explanation that other mathematicians can use. Demanding clarity is reasonable. Treating clarity as though it were the only evidence of correctness discounts the verification work already done.

The importance reaches beyond one celebrated problem. This episode offers a concrete model for AI-assisted discovery whose output can be checked independently of the system that helped produce it. The mathematical community’s next achievement may be to make the argument shorter, clearer and more useful. That prospect is a reason for excitement—and for giving both the result and its reviewers the attention they deserve.

title: SpaceX Catches Starship From Orbit for the First Time
excerpt: The first tower catch of Starship’s upper stage brings SpaceX closer to a fully reusable rocket—and gives its Moon and Mars ambitions a major engineering boost.
imageAlt: Starship and its launch tower illuminated at night at Starbase, with a foreground barrier reading WE ARE EXPLORERS
imageCaption: Archival photograph: Starship at Starbase on October 12, 2024, before Flight 5; this is not a photograph of the November 2026 catch. Photo by Steve Jurvetson, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY 2.0. Resized for the web; previews may crop the image.
content:
SpaceX brought a Starship upper stage home from orbit and caught it with the launch tower’s arms for the first time on November 14, 2026. The Flight 15 catch took place at Starbase in South Texas at about 3:20 p.m. local time, roughly 22.5 hours after launch. It is a remarkable achievement for the engineers working to make SpaceX’s largest rocket fly again and again. Space.com’s catch report

A new milestone for the ship

SpaceX had already caught a Super Heavy booster on October 13, 2024, during Flight 5. This time, the returning vehicle was the upper stage: Starship itself. The distinction matters because the company’s ambition is to recover and reuse both parts of the launch system. The earlier booster catch and the new ship catch mark separate steps toward that goal. SpaceX’s Flight 5 recap

Flight 15 did not achieve the planned recovery of both stages. Super Heavy’s catch was called off after a low-fuel alarm, and the booster diverted toward the Gulf of Mexico. That setback leaves SpaceX with work to do even as it celebrates the successful ship recovery. Flight 15 reporting

Why this achievement matters

SpaceX describes full and rapid reuse as fundamental to Starship’s design and its ambition to make life multiplanetary. Bringing the upper stage back to the launch site strengthens the engineering case for that vision. It gives the team recovered hardware to examine and a successful flight to learn from. SpaceX’s reusability goals

The economic promise is straightforward: if expensive flight hardware can be used repeatedly with limited refurbishment, its construction cost can be spread across more missions. Our assessment is that this catch makes that prospect more credible. It does not yet establish the cost of a Starship launch, the time needed to prepare a recovered ship, or the number of flights it can survive.

What comes next

The practical tests ahead are repeatability, recovery of both stages on the same mission, and successful reuse of the returned ship. Inspection and subsequent flights will matter as much as the dramatic moment at the tower. For SpaceX’s mission, the decisive advance will be turning an exceptional recovery into a dependable operating routine.

There is also a larger lunar architecture to prove. NASA’s October 2026 update describes a series of tanker Starships delivering propellant to a depot in Earth orbit before fueling the Starship lunar lander. Frequent, reliable launches could help make that sequence workable, but orbital propellant transfer and storage remain distinct engineering challenges. NASA also requires an uncrewed lander demonstration before a crewed lunar mission. NASA’s lunar lander plan

For supporters of SpaceX’s Moon and Mars ambitions, there is good reason for optimism. A reusable transport system needs hardware that can come home, and Starship has now demonstrated a crucial part of that journey. The next chapter is about proving it can keep doing so—and then fly again.

title: OpenAI Claims a Proof of Yang–Mills Existence
excerpt: A research group is checking OpenAI’s claimed proof that a four-dimensional quantum field theory exists. The proof remains private, and the mass gap is still open.
imageAlt: Separate black-and-white portraits of physicists Chen-Ning Yang on the left and Robert L. Mills on the right
imageCaption: Separate portraits of Chen-Ning Yang (left) and Robert L. Mills (right), cropped and arranged side by side. Yang portrait by the U.S. Department of Energy (public domain). Mills portrait by Peter A. Frisch. Yang photo · Mills photo · Composite licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.
content:
On October 26, OpenAI said its internal models had produced a proof that pure quantum Yang–Mills theory exists in four dimensions. The company dates the written argument to September 9 and says it completed a formal version in Lean, a computer proof assistant, on October 16. Clay still lists the full Millennium Prize problem as unsolved. OpenAI’s announcement · Clay Mathematics Institute

What has been made public

The working group led by physicist David Gross says the argument builds on Tadeusz Bałaban’s work on how gauge theories behave across scales. One way to start is to put the fields on a grid, where calculations have a built-in smallest distance. The hard part is showing that the grid can be made arbitrarily fine and the region arbitrarily large while retaining a well-defined, interacting theory. The group says OpenAI’s work reaches that continuum limit. Working group’s October statement

What remains unknown

As of November 4, the written argument and Lean files had yet to be made public. In a November 3 update, the group said it was checking whether the definitions and theorem in Lean match those used by physicists and mathematicians, and whether the formal version captures the written argument. It hopes to release the Lean files the following week if those checks are complete. A separate advisory group on mathematics and AI called for immediate release of both versions so the wider community could examine them. November 3 update · Advisory group’s October 26 statement

Lean can check the deductions from the definitions and assumptions it is given. Comparing the encoded theorem with the Clay problem requires a separate check. Clay asks for a nontrivial theory on all of four-dimensional Euclidean space, for every compact simple gauge group, a class of symmetries that includes SU(2) and SU(3). The public descriptions leave open which groups the argument covers, which axioms it establishes and how it controls the limits. Official problem statement by Arthur Jaffe and Edward Witten

Why the mass gap matters

Chen-Ning Yang and Robert Mills introduced their gauge theory in 1954. In the theory of the strong force, the force carriers are gluons, which interact with one another. Pure Yang–Mills isolates that interaction by leaving out matter fields such as quarks. The expectation is that these self-interactions generate a minimum energy for excitations above the vacuum even though the starting equations contain no explicit mass term. That minimum is the mass gap. It would also imply that correlations between local measurements in the vacuum decay exponentially with distance. Yang and Mills’s 1954 paper · Clay’s explanation of the mass gap

Computer calculations on lattices already give strong evidence for both the continuum theory and a gap. A verified construction would give mathematicians a precisely defined theory on which to test those predictions and could give them techniques for constructing other four-dimensional quantum field theories. The next public milestone is the Lean release, which would let researchers check what theorem the argument establishes. Working group’s assessment plan

title: OpenAI Publishes Results on Open Math Problems
excerpt: OpenAI's October 6 release shares AI-generated results on open research problems, alongside manuscripts and computer-checkable proofs for public scrutiny.
imageAlt: An abstract cyan and violet mathematical surface with a luminous wireframe mesh and connected nodes
imageCaption: AI-generated editorial illustration of mathematical research; not a visualization of a specific proof.
content:
On October 6, 2026, OpenAI announced a collection of new mathematical results produced by an unreleased internal model. It published the research on GitHub, giving mathematicians access to manuscripts and supporting proof materials.

A collection of new research

As of October 10, the public repository lists 719 manuscripts grouped into 372 families. Each family brings together related work, such as a principal result, companion arguments, consequences, or alternative proofs. These counts describe the collection, rather than a one-to-one tally of independently solved problems.

Making proofs checkable

The release includes formal proofs written in Lean, which lets a computer check mathematical arguments. The repository reports that roughly 42% of its top-line results have been formalized. OpenAI says it will add more formalizations as they become available.

OpenAI also released ten summaries of the model's reasoning, information about attempted problems, and estimates of computational effort. The company describes the average result as using compute equivalent to roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.

What still needs checking

The repository explicitly says its results are at different stages of verification and that some unformalized results could contain issues. It commits to preserving earlier versions and recording corrections. Readers should evaluate individual papers and their proof artifacts, rather than treating the entire release as settled mathematics.

For a closer look, read OpenAI's announcement and browse the manuscripts, formalizations, and revision history.

title: The Future of AI: Beyond Generative Models
excerpt: Researchers are exploring the next frontier of artificial intelligence, moving towards reasoning and autonomous decision-making systems.
content:
Generative AI has changed the world, but what comes next? Researchers at top institutions are now pivoting towards System 2 AI—systems capable of deliberate reasoning, planning, and self-correction.

The Limits of LLMs

Current Large Language Models (LLMs) are impressive at pattern matching but struggle with logical consistency and truthfulness. The next generation of AI aims to solve this by integrating symbolic reasoning with neural networks.

Autonomous Agents

We are also seeing the rise of autonomous agents that can perform complex tasks on behalf of users, from coding entire applications to managing supply chains.

title: Mars Colonization: The First 100 Days
excerpt: A detailed look at the survival plan for the first human settlers on the Red Planet, from habitat construction to resource management.
content:
The first human mission to Mars is slated for the late 2030s. The first 100 days will be critical for survival.

Habitat Construction

Upon landing, the crew's first priority will be to deploy 3D-printed habitats using Martian regolith. These structures must shield astronauts from lethal radiation and dust storms.

Water and Oxygen

Life support systems will rely on extracting water ice from the subsurface and splitting it into oxygen and hydrogen fuel.

title: CRISPR 2.0: Eradicating Genetic Diseases
excerpt: New gene-editing techniques promise to cure hereditary conditions with unprecedented precision and safety.
content:
CRISPR-Cas9 was just the beginning. New 'prime editing' techniques allow for search-and-replace editing of the genome without making double-strand breaks.

Targeting Sickle Cell

Clinical trials are already showing high success rates in curing Sickle Cell Anemia using these advanced methods.

title: Quantum Internet: A New Era of Security
excerpt: Scientists successfully teleport information across a metropolitan network, bringing the quantum internet one step closer to reality.
content: Quantum entanglement allows for unhackable communication. Recent experiments have successfully distributed quantum keys over 50 kilometers of standard fiber optic cable.

title: Deep Ocean Mysteries Revealed
excerpt: Autonomous submersibles discover new bioluminescent species in the Mariana Trench, challenging our understanding of life in the deep.
content: The deep ocean remains less explored than the surface of Mars. New autonomous drones are changing that, revealing a vibrant ecosystem thriving in total darkness.

title: The Search for Exoplanets Continues
excerpt: NASA's latest telescope captures images of a potentially habitable super-Earth in a nearby star system.
content: The James Webb Space Telescope has identified K2-18b, a planet in the habitable zone that shows strong signatures of water vapor and methane.
